name: ARM

claims.claim_text: Networking equipment remained a large MIPS market well after ARMv8 arrived, so MIPS skills still had commercial demand in that segment.
claims.quote_verbatim: my company is considering an offer because networking still uses the hell out of MIPS. And ARM V8 hasn't replaced it yet.
claims.episode_title: Back Into The Swing Of Things

claims.claim_text: Home chip fabrication is impractical because the chemical process steps require fabs that cost hundreds of millions of dollars at minimum, unlike the comparatively trivial mechanics of plastic extrusion.
claims.quote_verbatim: That's why these fab houses that make these chips cost hundreds of millions of dollars at a minimum.
claims.episode_title: Military Electronics and The Free Eagle (Freagle) Campaign

claims.claim_text: ARM's lineage traces to the Acorn machines of the 1980s rather than to any of the established microprocessor houses.
claims.quote_verbatim: not everyone knows that arm processors came from the original Acorn, computer back in the 80s, but that's its heritage
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Solar Cells, SparkFun, TSMC - The Detroit Debunking

claims.claim_text: The Microchip PIC16C84 of 1993 mattered because its EEPROM program memory ended the era of UV-erasable or one-time-programmable parts and of expensive in-circuit emulators for code changes.
claims.quote_verbatim: it was the first microcontroller that wasn't either UV erasable or one time programmable. It used eSquared Prom.
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Solar Cells, SparkFun, TSMC - The Detroit Debunking

claims.claim_text: Intel Atom parts out-ran contemporary ARM cores on raw throughput while losing on performance per watt, which is why they were pushed into tasks like HD video that ARM could not carry.
claims.quote_verbatim: I thought the Atom chips killed the ARM. Ones in terms of sheer performance. Maybe not in actual performance per power consumption
claims.episode_title: BASIC, Chip companies & Robots - Pernicious Projects, Puppies in Peril

claims.claim_text: One approach to speeding up managed-language runtimes is to convert interpreter functions into a hardware-accelerated instruction set rather than executing them sequentially on a general-purpose ARM core.
claims.quote_verbatim: so instead of doing it in a sequential processor like an arm processor they're going to do it in hardware
claims.episode_title: Bob Pease, Jim Williams - Posthumous Pease Porridge

claims.claim_text: Hardware Java execution engines such as picoJava and the aJ102 had been attempted before and never reached commercial use, mostly remaining designs or FPGA experiments.
claims.quote_verbatim: they've actually tried this with java that like just straight java before but to my knowledge this has never worked
claims.episode_title: Bob Pease, Jim Williams - Posthumous Pease Porridge

claims.claim_text: Early smartphones were pushed past a gigahertz mainly to render the graphical user interface, and that clock rate directly drove battery drain and thermal load.
claims.quote_verbatim: just to run the the graphical user interface on these smartphones yeah they're crazy so and that chews into the battery consumption and the heat and everything else
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Bob Pease, Jim Williams - Posthumous Pease Porridge

claims.claim_text: When HP could no longer source the original 12C calculator ASIC, they rebuilt the product around an ARM core and emulated the old processor so the untouched original ROM could run, because emulation either works or visibly fails and is far easier to prove correct than reimplementing every financial algorithm.
claims.quote_verbatim: they redesigned the whole architecture based on a new ARM chip, right? And then they got the original ROMs and they emulated the original processor so they could run the original ROM
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Biarchy Birthday Bavardage

claims.claim_text: The ARM-based calculator redesign wrecked battery life because the core was clocked at 30 MHz off a coin cell, drawing current in gulps the cell handles inefficiently.
claims.quote_verbatim: they ran the thing at 30 megahertz and it's powered from a coin cell battery and it takes gulps of current from the battery and it's very inefficient
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Biarchy Birthday Bavardage

claims.claim_text: Microchip deliberately picked MIPS over ARM for the PIC32 line as a differentiation play, since every competitor was already going ARM.
claims.quote_verbatim: They decided not to go with ARM because everyone else was doing ARM, so they wanted to be different and chose MIPS.
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Øyvind Janbu - Feracious Fabless Facilitator

claims.claim_text: A chip startup that picks a minority architecture burns its customer meetings justifying the architecture instead of selling the part's actual differentiators, which is a real sales cost.
claims.quote_verbatim: what you end up these days, I think, is to basically spend most of your customer meeting convincing people why MIPS is as good as ARM.
claims.speaker: Øyvind Janbu
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Øyvind Janbu - Feracious Fabless Facilitator

claims.claim_text: The decisive advantage of licensing ARM for a new chip is the surrounding tools and middleware ecosystem, not the core itself; a technically equivalent but less supported core loses on support.
claims.quote_verbatim: If you look at, say, the whole ecosystem of tools and middleware and everything, then you start to really gain a lot of advantages from choosing ARM rather than something which may be as good but not as well supported.
claims.speaker: Øyvind Janbu
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Øyvind Janbu - Feracious Fabless Facilitator

claims.claim_text: Published ARM per-chip royalty rates are startlingly small, on the order of fractions of a penny per part, with the licensee's cost concentrated in up-front NRE.
claims.quote_verbatim: It was fractions of pennies for chips, at least when I saw it.
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Øyvind Janbu - Feracious Fabless Facilitator

claims.claim_text: ARM was not structured to serve a broad customer base, so an unknown startup had to work through back channels just to find the right people to license a core from.
claims.quote_verbatim: ARM wasn't, at least at the time, set up to cover a broad market, right? They have a relatively limited amount of both customers and potential customers.
claims.speaker: Øyvind Janbu
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Øyvind Janbu - Feracious Fabless Facilitator

claims.claim_text: Most application-processor vendors license their graphics IP; Broadcom is unusual in designing its own 3D core in-house, which is what went into the BCM2835 alongside a later-added ARM core.
claims.quote_verbatim: we're quite unusual at Broadcom in that we don't license our 3D IP. And most AP vendors use licensed IP for their graphics course.
claims.speaker: Eben Upton
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Eben Upton - Morbus Moilsome MakerFaire

claims.claim_text: FPGA vendors moved back toward hard silicon, embedding ARM cores, transceivers, UARTs and other microcontroller peripherals into the fabric, because the prediction that cheap FPGAs would displace microcontrollers never materialised.
claims.quote_verbatim: So, they've had to go back to hard silicon. So, they're embedding ARM processors in FPGAs now.
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Proemial Passive Poiesis

claims.claim_text: By the early 2010s ARM held roughly 85 percent of the mobile processor market while Intel had shipped essentially nothing into phones.
claims.quote_verbatim: saying that ARM isn't a competitor who currently have 85% of the market or something.
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Bonkers Birthday Badinage

claims.claim_text: XMOS built hardware multithreading rather than licensing ARM: silicon that executes several threads concurrently removes the context-switch penalty that breaks a conventional sequential processor under many simultaneous tasks.
claims.quote_verbatim: if you had silicon that was actually doing multiple threads at the same time, it would be the equivalent of like a multi-core but actually integrated
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Gouging Green Gardyloo

claims.claim_text: ARM began as the Acorn RISC Machine and was initially a captive part: the only way to obtain the chip was to buy the computer it sat inside.
claims.quote_verbatim: Yeah, ARM stands for ACORN RISC machine. And they were certainly out ahead of us, but theirs was a captive product.
claims.speaker: Philip Frieden
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Philip Freidin - Xenodochial Xilinx Ex-Employee

claims.claim_text: "Rationalizing the product line" is vendor language for discontinuing slow-selling parts, and the part you designed in is disproportionately likely to be one of them.
claims.quote_verbatim: Uh, they rationalize their product line. It means they dump products that aren't selling.
claims.episode_title: Tektronix, ChipReport.tv, & the Signal Path - Temperative Tegmen Temperature

claims.claim_text: ARM sells cores rather than silicon: no part can be bought from ARM itself, which is precisely why a designer can buy nominally the same core from around twenty different chip vendors.
claims.quote_verbatim: You cannot go out and buy an ARM processor from the ARM company.
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Tektronix, ChipReport.tv, & the Signal Path - Temperative Tegmen Temperature

claims.claim_text: A vendor that abandons its proprietary cores for ARM enters a commodity fight where the only remaining lever is price against half a dozen equally equipped competitors.
claims.quote_verbatim: that's fine if you want to move to all arm. But you're up against six other different players. So you better win on price then.
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Distribution, Wozniak & Robots - Early Eight-bit Endgame

claims.claim_text: End customers do not select products for the core inside; what buyers of chips actually weigh is whether the tools work, whether they are bug-free, and whether the team already knows them.
claims.quote_verbatim: at the end of the day, nobody cares if it's ARM or not. Right. Most people do not give a shit.
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Distribution, Wozniak & Robots - Early Eight-bit Endgame

claims.claim_text: A chip vendor buying ARM outright would be funding its own competitors' supply, since those competitors, Apple included, license the same cores.
claims.quote_verbatim: They'd be foolish to buy ARM because then they'd be supporting their competitor as well who uses ARM, including Apple.
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Kickstarter, Open Source RC & Modelsource - Facinorous Financial Foulness

claims.claim_text: Changing ARM silicon vendors, or even moving between ARM families from the same vendor, is a substantial engineering effort rather than a drop-in swap.
claims.quote_verbatim: You've got to do significant engineering to change arm vendors. Or even the same vendor to a different arm product within the same vendor.
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Processors, CEOs & Soldering irons - Plentiful Perfunctory Programs

claims.claim_text: The commercial logic of licensing ARM is that a ready-made core removes the need to fund an in-house processor-architecture team.
claims.quote_verbatim: a lot of people are using arm because the licensing is there. And it's, you know, it's a good core to drop in. And you can get rid of all your overhead, also known as your engineers that work on processor architecture
claims.episode_title: Processors, CEOs & Soldering irons - Plentiful Perfunctory Programs

claims.claim_text: Moving a proprietary line onto ARM widens the addressable market but collapses unit economics, trading five-dollar parts for fifty-cent parts at near-zero margin.
claims.quote_verbatim: now we can sell parts to everyone. It's like, yeah, well, you can. But now you're going to sell them for, you know, 50 cents. Whereas you're selling them for five bucks before.
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Processors, CEOs & Soldering irons - Plentiful Perfunctory Programs

claims.claim_text: A "not recommended for new designs" status is effectively an end-of-life warning: expect roughly two to five years of continued supply and plan a replacement.
claims.quote_verbatim: Well, it's not recommended for new designs, but that's basically the death knell, right? That's like, okay, you get two or three or maybe five years, but you better watch your back
claims.episode_title: eReaders, datasheets & board assembly - Yearly Yeasty Yapping

claims.claim_text: With cheap ARM silicon on every dev board, the community and support around a board has become a stronger selection criterion than its published specifications.
claims.quote_verbatim: community matters, and it's starting to get where community matters much more than specs, because everything has these low-cost chips on them
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Hamvention, Arduino and Intel - Burdensome Background Battology

claims.claim_text: Early Bluetooth low energy systems-on-chip combined an ARM core, SRAM, baseband, encoding and radio in one part, drawing about 3.8 mA in receive and transmit, and that integration is what made cheap networked sensor nodes practical.
claims.quote_verbatim: Although it needs 3.8 milliamps for receiving and TX.
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Firmware, Netburner and Semiconductors - Chris's Capitalism Colloquy

claims.claim_text: The Zynq pairs a dual ARM Cortex-A9 running around a gigahertz with FPGA fabric plus hard logic memory controllers for DDR2 and DDR3 and high-speed serial transceivers.
claims.quote_verbatim: it's a dual, it's a dual ARM one gig processor, A9 processor
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Tesla, FPGAs and DigiKey - Zesty Zippy Zynq

claims.claim_text: The 8051's four register banks make context switching nearly free: a task is assigned a bank and switching means pointing the CPU at another bank, leaving all state in place, so cooperative multitasking fits in a few dozen lines where an ARM or AVR needs far more code.
claims.quote_verbatim: when you have to switch context, you just tell the CPU, you're no longer running in bank one. You're running in bank two right now. So everything is left into place.
claims.speaker: Vincent Himpe
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Vincent Himpe - Escaped Electron Elocution

claims.claim_text: By 2014 the cumulative installed base of ARM-powered chips had reached roughly 50 billion, with about 10 billion shipped in 2013 alone.
claims.quote_verbatim: There are now 50 billion ARM power chips in the world.
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Capacitors, Simulation and Closures - Deonerated Design Dealmaking

claims.claim_text: ARM's per-chip royalty is measured in tenths of a cent rather than cents, which is why enormous unit volumes translate into modest revenue.
claims.quote_verbatim: I know it's not like one cent per chip. It's like, you know, I think it's like tens of cents per chip. No, no, no, no. Oh, tenths. Tenths with an H in there of cents.
claims.episode_title: Capacitors, Simulation and Closures - Deonerated Design Dealmaking

claims.claim_text: The reason to reach for an ARM application processor over a plain microcontroller is usually the high-level requirements: an operating system, a large graphical display, and networking.
claims.quote_verbatim: you're probably choosing arm processor because you want to run a, yeah. And operating system. You want to drive a big graphical display and you want to network
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Let's Hear It For The Buoys - Vanishing Vessel Vexation

claims.claim_text: Choosing an ARM Cortex-M3 for a product meant a mature toolchain with roughly seven different vendor compilers to choose from.
claims.quote_verbatim: Because it was an ARM M3 Cortex. So, the ecosystem was very well developed.
claims.speaker: Eric Van Wyk
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Eric VanWyk - Meiotic Mountenance Mooshimeter

claims.claim_text: Highly integrated modern parts have vendor-proprietary footprints, so there is no second source for the physical package and each part choice becomes one large locked-in decision rather than many small reversible ones.
claims.quote_verbatim: There, there is no drop-in replacement because no one's literally allowed to use that footprint.
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: The Art Of Staying Interested In Electronics - Exponible Electronics Ennui

claims.claim_text: General-purpose cores like x86 and ARM excel at running an operating system, but the architectural baggage they carry caps their achievable high-performance math throughput, which is the argument for a specialised parallel core alongside them.
claims.quote_verbatim: if you're talking about high-performance math, all that baggage that's in the processor architecture, I mean, the same baggage that I found in the Tiger Shark, it's there, which means that you're never really going to reach the top level performance
claims.speaker: Andreas Olofsson
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Andreas Olofsson - Adapteva's Ampliative Abacus

claims.claim_text: Licensing a processor architecture is very hard without shipping the compiler and software stack with it; customers license a solution, not an ISA.
claims.quote_verbatim: what we found was that it's very hard to do the licensing of a processor architecture without having the software to go with it.
claims.speaker: Andreas Olofsson
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Andreas Olofsson - Adapteva's Ampliative Abacus

claims.claim_text: The working method on a heterogeneous ARM-plus-accelerator board is to run the application on the ARM core, identify the bottleneck section, split it into worker threads and dispatch one per accelerator core; the speedup is easy when threads do not communicate and much harder when they do.
claims.quote_verbatim: then you take some part of that application. That's the bottleneck. You'll send out, you, you'll divide that up into 16 work threads. You'll send each thread to, uh, to an epiphany core.
claims.speaker: Andreas Olofsson
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Andreas Olofsson - Adapteva's Ampliative Abacus

claims.claim_text: The claim that ARM lets you move freely between manufacturers is overstated; the move is possible but remains painful in practice.
claims.quote_verbatim: People crap on about ARM, you know. Oh, the good thing about ARM is that you can move from one manufacturer to it. It's bullshit.
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: No One Even Missed Us?

claims.claim_text: Microchip's CEO justified staying off ARM on the grounds that licensees pay an ARM royalty and get no point of differentiation for it.
claims.quote_verbatim: when I spoke to Steve Sangy, the CEO of Microchip, like five years ago, right? Yeah. He said exactly that. We don't want to get into arm because you've got to pay the arm tax
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Our Second Callin Show(ish)

claims.claim_text: Competition among ARM licensees drove part prices toward fifty cents and below, which undermines the business case for entering the market as yet another supplier.
claims.quote_verbatim: the cost of arms, these arm processors just keep dropping to dropping, dropping to where they're, they're 50 cents are almost free.
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Our Second Callin Show(ish)

claims.claim_text: For someone outgrowing 8-bit Arduino but wanting a hosted environment, ARM's mbed covering the Cortex line is a reasonable next step, though its debugging support is weak.
claims.quote_verbatim: The first one I would recommend would be the embed system. That's from ARM. And so it's all the Cortex processors.
claims.speaker: Elecia White
claims.episode_title: Crossovers and Call-ins

claims.claim_text: For driving a display, a general-purpose ARM part beats a DSP, and some ARM microcontrollers include an LCD controller peripheral outright.
claims.quote_verbatim: DSPs are really, really cool, but don't use them for what you've, you're better off using an arm for its general purposeness. And some of the arm controllers have LCD controllers as part of them.
claims.speaker: Elecia White
claims.episode_title: Crossovers and Call-ins

claims.claim_text: The bottom of the Cortex-M0 range and the top of the ATmega range do not overlap in capability: the smallest M0 already offers more, and an M4 adds floating point and DSP instructions.
claims.quote_verbatim: when you look at a cortex m0 the very bottom of the cortex m0s the very top of the at mega chips they don't overlap i mean you get a lot more in the cortex m0
claims.speaker: Elecia White
claims.episode_title: Crossovers and Call-ins

claims.claim_text: Reaching for an ARM part to blink a couple of LEDs is overkill when an eight-pin micro does the job.
claims.quote_verbatim: I hate using ARM when it's a couple LEDs because you could use a little 8-in micro.
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Timothy Lamb

claims.claim_text: ARM was chosen as the teaching architecture for an embedded course specifically because its longevity was safe enough to make the register-level and peripheral knowledge worth learning.
claims.quote_verbatim: the reason I chose ARM specifically, like, a lot of people ask, well, why don't you use, you know, this process or that process or whatever? I was like, look, I don't care what you think, ARM isn't going away for a little bit.
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Mergers and Acquiescence

claims.claim_text: Selling ARM-based microcontrollers is a low-margin, cutthroat business, which is a poor fit for a company whose other business units are used to high margins.
claims.quote_verbatim: people making ARM chips are not making a ton of margin, right? Oh, no. That's what's crazy. It's a cutthroat business.
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: The Automation Amish

claims.claim_text: Modern ARM parts let you write the bootstrap and startup code entirely in C, where older architectures such as Coldfire required hand-written assembly.
claims.quote_verbatim: it's basically the arm – the more modern arm chips. They are nice in that respect that you can actually write that stuff in C.
claims.speaker: Piotr Esden-Tempski
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Piotr Esden-Tempski

claims.claim_text: The ESP is a Tensilica core rather than ARM and runs FreeRTOS rather than Linux, because roughly half a megabyte of RAM keeps it in embedded territory.
claims.quote_verbatim: It's also not, not running Linux. It's running free artos. Uh, it's more of an embedded thing because you only have, well, you only have like in half a megabyte of RAM to work with.
claims.speaker: Jeroen Domburg
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Jeroen Domburg (Sprite_tm)

claims.claim_text: In a Zynq the ARM subsystem is a hard IP black box; the FPGA bitstream only configures how that block connects to user logic, so a vendor could in principle substitute a different hard core without changing the bitstream format.
claims.quote_verbatim: the arm is in hard IP block. Um, so only thing that the, uh, the bit stream does is configuring how these hard IP block connects to your logic.
claims.speaker: Claire Wolf
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Claire (née 'Clifford') Wolf

claims.claim_text: Building a processor is the easy part; the hard and valuable part is the compiler, debugger and tool ecosystem around it, which is why proprietary instruction sets are guarded as monopoly assets while benefiting from open-source tool developers.
claims.quote_verbatim: building a processor is actually very, very simple. The hard part usually is not building the processor. The hard part is building all the software tools around that processor.
claims.speaker: Claire Wolf
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Claire (née 'Clifford') Wolf

claims.claim_text: ARM shifted from long negotiations before anyone could even see the HDL to publishing downloadable M0 and M3 source, licensed for evaluation and integration but not for use in a shipped ASIC, so customers can start integrating while contracts are still being argued.
claims.quote_verbatim: of course it has a license that says you're not allowed to actually use it in an ASIC, but you can start playing around with it, integrating it right away
claims.speaker: Claire Wolf
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Claire (née 'Clifford') Wolf

claims.claim_text: A large fraction of an x86 die area goes to instruction decoding, which is why embedded parts favour RISC-style designs; ARM itself has not been a pure RISC design for a long time despite the name.
claims.quote_verbatim: a lot of the area in an x86 processor is actually dedicated to things like decoding instructions
claims.speaker: Claire Wolf
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Claire (née 'Clifford') Wolf

claims.claim_text: The speculative-execution vulnerabilities hit only specific ARM cores such as the Cortex-A8, A9, A17 and R8, leaving the low-power Cortex-M parts common in connected devices unaffected.
claims.quote_verbatim: not all arms are susceptible, only some, um, the Cortex R8, A8, A9, A17
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Debugger vs Printeffer

claims.claim_text: ARM's naming splits into architecture versions and core families: ARMv7 is the architecture the Cortex families derive from, while ARMv8 introduced the 64-bit generation.
claims.quote_verbatim: So the ARM-V7 variant is where all the Cortex families came from. Okay. Whereas the ARM-V8 is now the new 64-bit stuff.
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Jason Kridner and Robert Nelson

claims.claim_text: Ordinary Linux userspace C code, such as a serial-port utility, needs no knowledge of the underlying architecture and simply rebuilds from x86 to ARM.
claims.quote_verbatim: It's just generic C for talking to a serial port in Linux.
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Jason Kridner and Robert Nelson

claims.claim_text: Because nearly every chip company is now fabless, the shortage of open foundry capacity beyond TSMC is a real constraint, and an additional merchant foundry would shorten lead times.
claims.quote_verbatim: if Intel opened up and they're like, Hey, you can get some of our sweet foundry action. Right. Then, you know, lead times could go down
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Microfichery

claims.claim_text: ARM registered and ran a site arguing against RISC-V, treating the open instruction set as competition; RISC-V is an ISA rather than a processor, with distinct cores implemented against it.
claims.quote_verbatim: It was called riskv-basics.com. And. They basically was registered by Arm.
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Once Every Couple Months

claims.claim_text: A three-cent microcontroller is not compelling against a fifty-cent ARM part, because the saving is not an order of magnitude once the tooling burden is counted.
claims.quote_verbatim: I would go, well, no, I'm going to use a 50-cent ARM chip instead of 30 cents or a 60-cent, you know. Like, it's not the order of magnitude decrease in price
claims.speaker: Mike Harrison
claims.episode_title: 3 Cent Micros And 1000s of LEDs

claims.claim_text: The most popular low-end STM32 parts became hard to source precisely because everyone had standardised on them.
claims.quote_verbatim: I gather that some of the more popular lowest-end STMs are getting quite hard to get hold of now
claims.speaker: Mike Harrison
claims.episode_title: 3 Cent Micros And 1000s of LEDs

claims.claim_text: The MSP430 sits below ARM microcontrollers on both power and processing; a radio-integrated variant measured around three microamps, giving years of coin-cell life in a wristwatch build.
claims.quote_verbatim: it also gives you a 16-bit microcontroller that costs almost no power. I believe I'm measuring three microamps. So I get years of battery life on a coin cell.
claims.speaker: Travis Goodspeed
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Travis Goodspeed

claims.claim_text: Where the ARM microcontroller field was once too crowded to choose from, the STM32 became the default pick largely because everyone else had picked it.
claims.quote_verbatim: if you're coming in and going, I need to use an arm chip, that's probably the one you're going to choose just because of like everyone else is using it
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Bill and Dave's Excellent Equipment

claims.claim_text: GigaDevices ships both a register-compatible STM32F103 clone and a RISC-V part whose name differs by a single letter, so GD32F103 and GD32VF103 are entirely different architectures.
claims.quote_verbatim: Giga devices decided it was a smart idea to make a completely different architecture part by changing one letter.
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Boat Anchors

claims.claim_text: ARM opened up custom instruction extensions for embedded cores as a direct answer to customers now being able to build their own processors under an open ISA.
claims.quote_verbatim: They're basically being like, oh, you wanted custom? We didn't know. Now you can be custom too, right?
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Boat Anchors

claims.claim_text: Reverse-engineering consumer devices is tractable largely because most are ARM-based, so mature disassembly tooling plus SWD or JTAG access is enough to patch and reflash firmware.
claims.quote_verbatim: we're benefiting from the fact that most of these devices are ARM-based. And there are lots of really good tools for working with ARM CPUs and ARM firmwares.
claims.speaker: Trammell Hudson
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Trammell Hudson

claims.claim_text: Before RISC-V, soft cores from open repositories were either legally encumbered against use in a product that grew large, or maintained by one person with an unmainlined GCC fork years out of date.
claims.quote_verbatim: it was really hard to get an IP that was unencumbered by, if I use this in a product that grows anywhere near big, then I will have Intel or ARM or whatever.
claims.speaker: Jeroen Domburg
claims.episode_title: Stories from Supercon 2019

claims.claim_text: A Zynq boots differently from an ordinary FPGA: the dual Cortex-A9 comes up first over JTAG and the ARM side then brings up the FPGA fabric, so bring-up order is ARM, then debug UART, then U-Boot in boot flash, then Linux.
claims.quote_verbatim: They actually boot up the dual Cortex-A9, and that ARM part of the chip actually controls bringing up the FPGA side.
claims.speaker: Craig J Bishop
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Craig J Bishop

claims.claim_text: AXI, the ARM-originated bus standard used heavily in Xilinx FPGAs, is intricate enough that hand-written Verilog needs a vendor verification model to check it; a higher-level HDL with a standard library that supplies a pre-verified AXI slave removes most of that work.
claims.quote_verbatim: So AXE is the bus standard used a lot in FPGAs, at least by Xilinx. And it's a complicated bus protocol. It comes from ARM and it has a lot of stuff you have to get right.
claims.speaker: Craig J Bishop
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Craig J Bishop

claims.claim_text: Cortex-M parts became cheap and capable enough that using an 8-bit part in a product that is not extremely price-sensitive is hard to justify when megabytes of memory cost a couple of dollars more.
claims.quote_verbatim: Why would you drop an 8-bitter into an application that's being sold for a lot of money? It just doesn't make a whole lot of sense today when you're getting megabytes of memory and all this kind of stuff on an MCU for just a couple of bucks more.
claims.speaker: Jack Ganssle
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Jack Ganssle (2nd)

claims.claim_text: ARM will license its IP free until a startup has a system running, which lowers the barrier for small companies to produce their own silicon and specialised parts.
claims.quote_verbatim: And ARM, actually, will license you their IP for free, at least until you get started, get your system up and going.
claims.speaker: Jack Ganssle
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Jack Ganssle (2nd)

claims.claim_text: Toolchain maturity, not the instruction set, is what should drive architecture selection; the 8051 and ARM chains are long proven, which is why risk-averse engineers stay with them.
claims.quote_verbatim: You have to worry about the tool chains, kind of Uber-alas. And the tool chains for the 8051, the ARM, all these other parts are well proven and have been around for a long time.
claims.speaker: Jack Ganssle
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Jack Ganssle (2nd)

claims.claim_text: An open silicon design platform negotiated a blanket agreement letting users instantiate an ARM M0 core and simulate a full system in minutes without contacting ARM, with the RTL kept behind the platform rather than downloadable.
claims.quote_verbatim: today we have an agreement with ARM. You can actually get to our platform, use the one of their cores, like the M0, without talking to ARM.
claims.speaker: Mohamed Kassem
claims.episode_title: Fabless Chip Design with Mohamed Kassem

claims.claim_text: A fab cannot carry its capital cost on manufacturing alone; the IP and brand side is where the margin sits, which is why splitting process from design is harder than it looks.
claims.quote_verbatim: you would never be able to support just the cost, the high capital costs of a fab without all the, you know, the smooshy IP side of things
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: This Is Just A Tribute

claims.claim_text: The RP2040 is a Cortex-M0 microcontroller that Raspberry Pi designed themselves rather than an off-the-shelf part, and it is not a Linux-class application processor.
claims.quote_verbatim: It's called the RP 2040 is the chip, which raspberry pie have. They've actually developed this chip.
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: New Year, New Gear

claims.claim_text: A modern video-mixing SoC can carry six hard ARM cores split between application processors and real-time cores, mixing an A53-class core with Cortex-M-class parts on one die.
claims.quote_verbatim: It's got four applications processors, as they call it, applications in quote marks. And it's got two, or it might be the other way around, two real-time processors.
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Recalling Recalls

claims.claim_text: MIPS, the architecture Microchip famously picked over ARM for the PIC32, later abandoned its own architecture and rebased its next generation on the open RISC-V standard.
claims.quote_verbatim: the official statement says, we're developing a new industry leading standards, eighth generation architecture, which we will be basing on the open source risk five processor standard
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Firmware Update Capabilities

claims.claim_text: A perpetual architecture licence protects the licensee if the architecture owner fails: the rights are bought outright so production continues regardless of the licensor's solvency.
claims.quote_verbatim: It was like, we're licensing your architecture. We want it forever. Here's the money. Bugger off. If you guys go under, that's your business.
claims.episode_title: Firmware Update Capabilities

claims.claim_text: Migrating a product family to ARM to unlock features like Bluetooth firmware update and SD card support is pure sunk engineering cost, because customers will not pay extra for the architecture change itself.
claims.quote_verbatim: your, your client's not going to pay more for that. The feature of being on arm now.
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: NFT Schematics

claims.claim_text: A Cortex-M0 was implemented in polymer-based plastic transistors as an ultra-minimal system-on-chip with 128 bytes of RAM and 456 bytes of ROM.
claims.quote_verbatim: ultra minimalist Cortex M zero base sock with 128 bytes of Ram and 466, 456 bytes of ROM
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Feed the Mouse

claims.claim_text: The awkward chained clock enabling on ST parts is an ARM-wide consequence of the high-speed and low-speed bus split: each peripheral takes a different clock source and PLLs must be enabled to reach higher frequencies, so a missed enable leaves the peripheral silently dead.
claims.quote_verbatim: it's an ARM thing because of the high speed bus, low speed bus, all the peripherals gets a different clock source.
claims.speaker: Orkhan Amiraslanov
claims.episode_title: Generic Nodes with Orkhan Amiraslanov

claims.claim_text: Chinese ownership rules blocking foreign majority control forced ARM to spin its China operation into a separate company that is not part of ARM proper.
claims.quote_verbatim: It is not part of the arm company. They basically had to split it off.
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Toasted Marshmallow Connectors

claims.claim_text: "Experience with ARM" is too broad to be a hiring signal; naming a specific family and toolchain, such as an STM32 F0 or L0 flow, demonstrates immediately usable skill.
claims.quote_verbatim: I've got experience in arm. Right. They try and like, it's like, yeah, that's pretty broad brush. That's pretty like, yeah, that's not really a useful skill in its own right.
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Here for a reason

claims.claim_text: Raspberry Pi began selling the RP2040 in reels at 80 cents per unit for 500 pieces and 70 cents for 3,400 pieces, after demand for the bare chip reached tens of thousands of units.
claims.quote_verbatim: So you can buy 500, a reel of 500 of them for at a unit price of 80 cents, or you can buy a reel of 3,400 for 70 cents.
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Bubblegum Tap Shoes

claims.claim_text: Regulators blocked a chip company acquiring ARM because so many ARM licensees compete with the acquirer, creating both IP-access and preferential-treatment concerns.
claims.quote_verbatim: there was too much regulatory issue because companies, you know, there's so many companies that use Arm, which are competitors to them.
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Histogrammic or Histomagraphical

claims.claim_text: ARM's secure-world design deliberately requires very specific instruction sequences to cross between secure and non-secure state, so that an unintended transition cannot happen by accident.
claims.quote_verbatim: you end up having to do very specific sequences to be able to transition between secure and, uh, non-secure world. And this is actually well-designed, um, on ARM's part
claims.speaker: Laura Abbott
claims.episode_title: Finding Hardware Flaws with Laura Abbott

claims.claim_text: Whether Rust is usable on a given microcontroller comes down to two checks: whether the chip architecture has general toolchain support, and whether crate-level register access exists for that part.
claims.quote_verbatim: the first big question about is, is that what chip architecture are you actually running on? And is there a tool chain support in general for that?
claims.speaker: Laura Abbott
claims.episode_title: Finding Hardware Flaws with Laura Abbott

claims.claim_text: Obtaining a large physically contiguous block of memory is a genuinely hard kernel problem, which is why Linux on ARM needed the contiguous memory allocator alongside ordinary page allocation.
claims.quote_verbatim: It turns out that solving the problem about, I want to get a large physical chunk of contiguous memory is actually a pretty difficult problem to solve on a, on a system.
claims.speaker: Laura Abbott
claims.episode_title: Finding Hardware Flaws with Laura Abbott

claims.claim_text: Adding an Infineon 43439 Wi-Fi part to the RP2040 board raised its price by about two dollars.
claims.quote_verbatim: now it has a, uh, Infineon four, three, four, three, nine wifi chip on it. And that's basically that upped it by $2
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Trade Show or Conference?

claims.claim_text: Concentration on a single popular ARM family creates its own supply risk, with STM32 parts unobtainable at the same time as PIC parts during the shortage.
claims.quote_verbatim: I don't want to do the STM 32 thing. That's like grown, you know, like you can't get them and everyone's doing the stupid arm thing.
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Best way to find a leak

claims.claim_text: Companies like Qualcomm and Broadcom build very large ASICs whose value lies in the surrounding blocks wrapped around licensed ARM IP, and handset makers have been buying up those capabilities to bring them in-house.
claims.quote_verbatim: you think about the value add on top of like an ARM processor that a Qualcomm and a Broadcom is doing, right? They're, they're doing these huge, huge ASICs that have IP from ARM
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Conference Room Innovation

claims.claim_text: A cheaper 32-bit ARM part is hard to beat for an embedded design that is not strongly cost-constrained, unless the application specifically needs something an FPGA provides.
claims.quote_verbatim: it's really hard to beat that, you know, unless you need something specific from like an FPGA or something, it's like, why don't you just use, you know, that cheap 32 bit arm
claims.speaker: Jeremiah Gillis
claims.episode_title: More Electronics Consultant Impedance Matching

claims.claim_text: An ARM royalty looks negligible per unit but becomes material at ten million chips, which is why a RISC-V consortium functions partly as leverage on ARM's pricing.
claims.quote_verbatim: it doesn't look like a lot on paper, but when you add it all up and you look at, Oh, when you make a 10 million chips, it matters.
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Sad Violins for Superconductors

claims.claim_text: RP2040 uses a small bus fabric tuned for low latency so a peripheral read takes one or two clock cycles, whereas the PCI Express based RP1 fabric trades latency for throughput and a peripheral access can take around ten cycles, which is acceptable under Linux.
claims.quote_verbatim: RP2040 has got a really small bus fabric that's designed for, like, low latency. So if you want to go and read a peripheral, that will take one or two clock cycles on RP2040.
claims.speaker: Liam Fraser
claims.episode_title: The RP1 and beyond with the Raspberry Pi Hardware team

claims.claim_text: Successive Raspberry Pi generations absorbed external control silicon into the main chips, which lowers overall cost, simplifies the supply chain, and frees increasingly scarce board area.
claims.quote_verbatim: One is it lowers the cost in general. And it also makes your supply chain a bit simpler.
claims.speaker: James Adams
claims.episode_title: The RP1 and beyond with the Raspberry Pi Hardware team

claims.claim_text: ARM IP is chosen for new silicon because it is easy to obtain, well tested, well documented and available in genuinely high-performance cores, with no equivalent RISC-V option and a large software-maturity gap behind x86 and ARM.
claims.quote_verbatim: But in general, it's very easy to get hold of ARM IP. It works very well. It's well tested. It's well documented.
claims.speaker: James Adams
claims.episode_title: The RP1 and beyond with the Raspberry Pi Hardware team

claims.claim_text: A 128-core Windows-on-ARM desktop tops the 2024 Cinebench results while only exercising 64 cores, because the benchmark has a defect above 64 cores on ARM that previously also affected high-core-count x86 systems.
claims.quote_verbatim: The Cinebench has a weird bug running on more than 64 cores on arm.
claims.speaker: Jeff Geerling
claims.episode_title: Learning Computing with Jeff Geerling

claims.claim_text: With mature build systems and hardware abstraction layers in place, day-to-day microcontroller work looks the same on a RISC-V core as on an ARM core; the architecture only surfaces in the toolchain names.
claims.quote_verbatim: the way I operate with microcontrollers these days, I couldn't tell the difference between a risk five and a, you know, arm core
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Small Scale Electronics Manufacturing with Colin O'Flynn

claims.claim_text: RISC architectures such as ARM win by deleting the transistors and architectural machinery that exist only to support a complex instruction set and backward compatibility.
claims.quote_verbatim: because you eliminate a ton of useless architecture issues and transistors and things like that, that were created to support a rather complex instruction set
claims.speaker: Jerry Twomey
claims.episode_title: Applied Embedded Electronics with Jerry Twomey

claims.claim_text: ARM's first designs shipped inside the BBC Micro and the name stands for Acorn RISC Machine; the company then went decades selling only IP before shipping a chip of its own.
claims.quote_verbatim: They were originally in the BBC micro, right? That was where they first started. And arm stands for acorn risk machine.
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Hyper Growth and OpenClaw Interns

claims.claim_text: The first 32-bit Arduino board was built on an ARM processor sourced from Atmel, later part of Microchip.
claims.quote_verbatim: we did the first product using an ARM processor from Atmel, then they became microchip.
claims.speaker: Massimo Banzi
claims.episode_title: Arduino's Invisible Touch with Massimo Banzi

claims.claim_text: ARM Limited lent Arduino the money needed to regain control of the company during an internal takeover fight, an ecosystem investment that also carried real risk for the lender.
claims.quote_verbatim: when I needed someone to give me some money, lend me some money to actually take back control of the company
claims.speaker: Massimo Banzi
claims.episode_title: Arduino's Invisible Touch with Massimo Banzi
